{{Short description|Theorem in analysis}}
: ''For other inequalities named after Wirtinger, see [[Wirtinger's inequality (disambiguation)|Wirtinger's inequality]].''

In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[mathematical analysis|analysis]], the '''Wirtinger inequality''' is an important inequality for functions of a single variable, named after [[Wilhelm Wirtinger]]. It was used by [[Adolf Hurwitz]] in 1901 to give a new proof of the [[isoperimetric inequality]] for curves in the plane.  A variety of closely related results are today known as Wirtinger's inequality, all of which can be viewed as certain forms of the [[Poincaré inequality]].

==Theorem==
There are several inequivalent versions of the Wirtinger inequality:
* Let {{mvar|y}} be a continuous and [[differentiable function]] on the interval {{math|{{closed-closed|0, ''L''}}}} with average value zero and with {{math|''y''(0) {{=}} ''y''(''L'')}}. Then
::<math>\int_0^L y(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x\leq\frac{L^2}{4\pi^2}\int_0^L y'(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x,</math>
: and equality holds if and only if {{math|''y''(''x'') {{=}} ''c'' sin {{sfrac|2&pi;(''x'' − &alpha;)|''L''}}}} for some numbers {{mvar|c}} and {{math|&alpha;}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Hardy|1a2=Littlewood|1a3=Pólya|1y=1952|1loc=Section 7.7}}
* Let {{mvar|y}} be a continuous and differentiable function on the interval {{math|{{closed-closed|0, ''L''}}}} with {{math|''y''(0) {{=}} ''y''(''L'') {{=}} 0}}. Then
::<math>\int_0^L y(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x\leq\frac{L^2}{\pi^2}\int_0^L y'(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x,</math>
: and equality holds if and only if {{math|''y''(''x'') {{=}} ''c'' sin {{sfrac|&pi;''x''|''L''}}}} for some number {{mvar|c}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Hardy|1a2=Littlewood|1a3=Pólya|1y=1952|1loc=Section 7.7}}
* Let {{mvar|y}} be a continuous and differentiable function on the interval {{math|{{closed-closed|0, ''L''}}}} with average value zero. Then
::<math>\int_0^L y(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x\leq \frac{L^2}{\pi^2}\int_0^L y'(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x.</math>
: and equality holds if and only if {{math|''y''(''x'') {{=}} ''c'' cos {{sfrac|&pi;''x''|''L''}}}} for some number {{mvar|c}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Brezis|1y=2011|1pp=511–513, 576–578}}
Despite their differences, these are closely related to one another, as can be seen from the account given below in terms of [[spectral geometry]]. They can also all be regarded as special cases of various forms of the [[Poincaré inequality]], with the optimal ''Poincaré constant'' identified explicitly. The middle version is also a special case of the [[Friedrichs inequality]], again with the optimal constant identified.

===Proofs===
The three versions of the Wirtinger inequality can all be proved by various means. This is illustrated in the following by a different kind of proof for each of the three Wirtinger inequalities given above. In each case, by a linear [[Integration by substitution|change of variables]] in the integrals involved, there is no loss of generality in only proving the theorem for one particular choice of {{mvar|L}}.

====Fourier series====
Consider the first Wirtinger inequality given above. Take {{mvar|L}} to be {{math|2&pi;}}. Since [[Dirichlet's conditions]] are met, we can write
:<math>y(x)=\frac{1}{2}a_0+\sum_{n\ge 1}\left(a_n\frac{\sin nx}{\sqrt{\pi}}+b_n\frac{\cos nx}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right),</math>
and the fact that the average value of {{mvar|y}} is zero means that {{math|''a''<sub>0</sub> {{=}} 0}}. By [[Parseval's identity]],

:<math>\int_0^{2\pi}y(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x=\sum_{n=1}^\infty(a_n^2+b_n^2)</math>

and

:<math>\int_0^{2\pi}y'(x)^2 \,\mathrm{d}x = \sum_{n=1}^\infty n^2(a_n^2+b_n^2)</math>

and since the summands are all nonnegative, the Wirtinger inequality is proved. Furthermore, it is seen that equality holds if and only if {{math|''a<sub>n</sub>'' {{=}} ''b<sub>n</sub>'' {{=}} 0}} for all {{math|''n'' ≥ 2}}, which is to say that {{math|''y''(''x'') {{=}} ''a''<sub>1</sub> sin ''x'' + ''b''<sub>1</sub> cos ''x''}}. This is equivalent to the stated condition by use of the [[List of trigonometric identities|trigonometric addition formulas]].

====Integration by parts====
Consider the second Wirtinger inequality given above.{{sfnm|1a1=Hardy|1a2=Littlewood|1a3=Pólya|1y=1952|1loc=Section 7.7}} Take {{mvar|L}} to be {{math|&pi;}}. Any differentiable function {{math|''y''(''x'')}} satisfies the identity
:<math>y(x)^2+\big(y'(x)-y(x)\cot x\big)^2=y'(x)^2-\frac{d}{dx}\big(y(x)^2\cot x\big).</math>
Integration using the [[fundamental theorem of calculus]] and the boundary conditions {{math|''y''(0) {{=}} ''y''(&pi;) {{=}} 0}} then shows
:<math>\int_0^\pi y(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x+\int_0^\pi\big(y'(x)-y(x)\cot x\big)^2\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_0^\pi y'(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x.</math>
This proves the Wirtinger inequality, since the second integral is clearly nonnegative. Furthermore, equality in the Wirtinger inequality is seen to be equivalent to {{math|''y''′(''x'') {{=}} ''y''(''x'') cot ''x''}}, the general solution of which (as computed by [[separation of variables]]) is {{math|''y''(''x'') {{=}} ''c'' sin ''x''}} for an arbitrary number {{mvar|c}}.

There is a subtlety in the above application of the fundamental theorem of calculus, since it is not the case that {{math|''y''(''x'')<sup>2</sup> cot ''x''}} extends continuously to {{math|''x'' {{=}} 0}} and {{math|''x'' {{=}} &pi;}} for every function {{math|''y''(''x'')}}. This is resolved as follows. It follows from the [[Hölder inequality]] and {{math|''y''(0) {{=}} 0}} that
:<math>|y(x)|=\left|\int_0^x y'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\right|\leq\int_0^x |y'(x)|\cdot1\,\mathrm{d}x\leq\left(\int_0^x1^2\mathrm{d}x\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_0^x y'(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x\right)^{1/2}=\sqrt{x}\left(\int_0^x y'(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x\right)^{1/2},</math>
which shows that as long as
:<math>\int_0^\pi y'(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x</math>
is finite, the limit of {{math|{{sfrac|1|''x''}} ''y''(''x'')<sup>2</sup>}} as {{mvar|x}} converges to zero is zero. Since {{math|cot ''x'' < {{sfrac|1|''x''}}}} for small positive values of {{mvar|x}}, it follows from the [[squeeze theorem]] that {{math|''y''(''x'')<sup>2</sup> cot ''x''}} converges to zero as {{mvar|x}} converges to zero. In exactly the same way, it can be proved that {{math|''y''(''x'')<sup>2</sup> cot ''x''}} converges to zero as {{mvar|x}} converges to {{math|&pi;}}.

====Functional analysis====
Consider the third Wirtinger inequality given above. Take {{mvar|L}} to be {{math|1}}. Given a continuous function {{mvar|f}} on {{math|{{closed-closed|0, 1}}}} of average value zero, let {{math|''Tf''}} denote the function {{mvar|u}} on {{math|{{closed-closed|0, 1}}}} which is of average value zero, and with {{math|''u''′′ + ''f'' {{=}} 0}} and {{math|''u''′(0) {{=}} ''u''′(1) {{=}} 0}}. From basic analysis of [[linear differential equation|ordinary differential equations with constant coefficients]], the eigenvalues of {{mvar|T}} are {{math|(''k''&pi;)<sup>−2</sup>}} for nonzero integers {{mvar|k}}, the largest of which is then {{math|&pi;<sup>−2</sup>}}. Because {{mvar|T}} is a bounded and [[self-adjoint operator]], it follows that
:<math>\int_0^1 Tf(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x\leq\pi^{-2}\int_0^1 f(x)Tf(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{\pi^2}\int_0^1 (Tf)'(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x</math>
for all {{mvar|f}} of average value zero, where the equality is due to [[integration by parts]]. Finally, for any continuously differentiable function {{mvar|y}} on {{math|{{closed-closed|0, 1}}}} of average value zero, let {{math|''g''<sub>''n''</sub>}} be a sequence of [[Support (mathematics)|compactly supported]] continuously differentiable functions on {{math|{{open-open|0, 1}}}} which converge in {{math|L<sup>2</sup>}} to {{math|''y''′}}. Then define
:<math>y_n(x)=\int_0^x g_n(z)\,\mathrm{d}z-\int_0^1 \int_0^w g_n(z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}w.</math>
Then each {{math|''y''<sub>''n''</sub>}} has average value zero with {{math|''y''<sub>''n''</sub>′(0) {{=}} ''y''<sub>''n''</sub>′(1) {{=}} 0}}, which in turn implies that {{math|−''y''<sub>''n''</sub>′′}} has average value zero. So application of the above inequality to {{math|''f'' {{=}} −''y''<sub>''n''</sub>′′}} is legitimate and shows that
:<math>\int_0^1 y_n(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x\leq\frac{1}{\pi^2}\int_0^1 y_n'(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x.</math>
It is possible to replace {{math|''y''<sub>''n''</sub>}} by {{mvar|y}}, and thereby prove the Wirtinger inequality, as soon as it is verified that {{math|''y''<sub>''n''</sub>}} converges in {{math|L<sup>2</sup>}} to {{math|''y''}}. This is verified in a standard way, by writing
:<math>y(x)-y_n(x)=\int_0^x \big(y_n'(z)-g_n(z)\big)\,\mathrm{d}z-\int_0^1\int_0^w (y_n'(z)-g_n(z)\big)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}w</math>
and applying the Hölder or Jensen inequalities.

This proves the Wirtinger inequality. In the case that {{math|''y''(''x'')}} is a function for which equality in the Wirtinger inequality holds, then a standard argument in the [[calculus of variations]] says that {{mvar|y}} must be a [[weak solution]] of the [[Euler–Lagrange equation]] {{math|''y''′′(''x'') + ''y''(''x'') {{=}} 0}} with {{math|''y''′(0) {{=}} ''y''′(1) {{=}} 0}}, and the [[regularity theory]] of such equations, followed by the usual analysis of [[linear differential equation|ordinary differential equations with constant coefficients]], shows that {{math|''y''(''x'') {{=}} ''c'' cos &pi;''x''}} for some number {{mvar|c}}.

To make this argument fully formal and precise, it is necessary to be more careful about the [[function space]]s in question.{{sfnm|1a1=Brezis|1y=2011|1pp=511–513, 576–578}}

==Spectral geometry==
In the language of [[spectral geometry]], the three versions of the Wirtinger inequality above can be rephrased as theorems about the first [[eigenvalue]] and corresponding [[eigenfunction]]s of the [[Laplace–Beltrami operator]] on various one-dimensional [[Riemannian manifold]]s:{{sfnm|1a1=Chavel|1y=1984|1loc=Sections I.3 and I.5}}
* the first eigenvalue of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the [[Riemannian circle]] of length {{math|''L''}} is {{math|{{sfrac|4&pi;<sup>2</sup>|''L''<sup>2</sup>}}}}, and the corresponding eigenfunctions are the linear combinations of the two coordinate functions.
* the first [[Dirichlet eigenvalue]] of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the interval {{math|{{closed-closed|0, ''L''}}}} is {{math|{{sfrac|&pi;<sup>2</sup>|''L''<sup>2</sup>}}}} and the corresponding eigenfunctions are given by {{math|''c'' sin {{sfrac|&pi;''x''|''L''}}}} for arbitrary nonzero numbers {{mvar|c}}.
* the first Neumann eigenvalue of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the interval {{math|{{closed-closed|0, ''L''}}}} is {{math|{{sfrac|&pi;<sup>2</sup>|''L''<sup>2</sup>}}}} and the corresponding eigenfunctions are given by {{math|''c'' cos {{sfrac|&pi;''x''|''L''}}}} for arbitrary nonzero numbers {{mvar|c}}.

These can also be extended to statements about higher-dimensional spaces. For example, the Riemannian circle may be viewed as the one-dimensional version of either a [[sphere]], [[real projective space]], or [[torus]] (of arbitrary dimension). The Wirtinger inequality, in the first version given here, can then be seen as the {{math|''n'' {{=}} 1}} case of any of the following:
* the first eigenvalue of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the unit-radius {{mvar|n}}-dimensional sphere is {{mvar|n}}, and the corresponding eigenfunctions are the linear combinations of the {{math|''n'' + 1}} coordinate functions.{{sfnm|1a1=Stein|1a2=Weiss|1y=1971|1loc=Chapter IV.2}}
* the first eigenvalue of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the {{mvar|n}}-dimensional real projective space (with normalization given by the [[covering map]] from the unit-radius sphere) is {{math|2''n'' + 2}}, and the corresponding eigenfunctions are the restrictions of the homogeneous quadratic polynomials on {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n'' + 1</sup>}} to the [[unit sphere]] (and then to the real projective space).{{sfnm|1a1=Chavel|1y=1984|1p=36}}
* the first eigenvalue of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the {{mvar|n}}-dimensional torus (given as the {{mvar|n}}-fold product of the circle of length {{math|2&pi;}} with itself) is {{math|1}}, and the corresponding eigenfunctions are arbitrary linear combinations of {{mvar|n}}-fold products of the eigenfunctions on the circles.{{sfnm|1a1=Chavel|1y=1984|1loc=Section II.2}}

The second and third versions of the Wirtinger inequality can be extended to statements about first Dirichlet and Neumann eigenvalues of the Laplace−Beltrami operator on [[metric ball]]s in [[Euclidean space]]:
* the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of the Laplace−Beltrami operator on the unit ball in {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} is the square of the smallest positive zero of the [[Bessel function|Bessel function of the first kind]] {{math|''J''<sub>(''n'' − 2)/2</sub>}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Chavel|1y=1984|1loc=Theorem II.5.4}}
* the first Neumann eigenvalue of the Laplace−Beltrami operator on the unit ball in {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} is the square of the smallest positive zero of the first derivative of the [[Bessel function|Bessel function of the first kind]] {{math|''J''<sub>''n''/2</sub>}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Chavel|1y=1984|1loc=Theorem II.5.4}}

==Application to the isoperimetric inequality==
In the first form given above, the Wirtinger inequality can be used to prove the [[isoperimetric inequality]] for curves in the plane, as found by [[Adolf Hurwitz]] in 1901.{{sfnm|1a1=Hardy|1a2=Littlewood|1a3=Pólya|1y=1952|1loc=Section 7.7|2a1=Hurwitz|2y=1901}} Let {{math|(''x'', ''y'')}} be a differentiable embedding of the circle in the plane. Parametrizing the circle by {{math|{{closed-closed|0, 2&pi;}}}} so that {{math|(''x'', ''y'')}} has constant speed, the length {{math|''L''}} of the curve is given by
:<math>\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{x'(t)^2+y'(t)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t</math>
and the area {{mvar|A}} enclosed by the curve is given (due to [[Stokes theorem]]) by
:<math>-\int_0^{2\pi}y(t)x'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.</math>
Since the integrand of the integral defining {{mvar|L}} is assumed constant, there is
:<math>\frac{L^2}{2\pi}-2A=\int_0^{2\pi}\big(x'(t)^2+y'(t)^2+2y(t)x'(t)\big)\,\mathrm{d}t</math>
which can be rewritten as
:<math>\int_0^{2\pi}\big(x'(t)+y(t)\big)^2\,\mathrm{d}t+\int_0^{2\pi}\big(y'(t)^2-y(t)^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}t.</math>
The first integral is clearly nonnegative. Without changing the area or length of the curve, {{math|(''x'', ''y'')}} can be replaced by {{math|(''x'', ''y'' + ''z'')}} for some number {{mvar|z}}, so as to make {{mvar|y}} have average value zero. Then the Wirtinger inequality can be applied to see that the second integral is also nonnegative, and therefore
:<math>\frac{L^2}{4\pi}\geq A,</math>
which is the isoperimetric inequality. Furthermore, equality in the isoperimetric inequality implies both equality in the Wirtinger inequality and also the equality {{math|''x''′(''t'') + ''y''(''t'') {{=}} 0}}, which amounts to {{math|''y''(''t'') {{=}} ''c''<sub>1</sub> sin(''t'' – &alpha;)}} and then {{math|''x''(''t'') {{=}} ''c''<sub>1</sub> cos(''t'' – &alpha;) + ''c''<sub>2</sub>}} for arbitrary numbers {{math|''c''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''c''<sub>2</sub>}}. These equations mean that the image of {{math|(''x'', ''y'')}} is a round circle in the plane.
